Ranchi: Increasing heat coupled with frequent heatwaves is taking a toll on human productivity in Jharkhand. A recent study by the Centre for Environment and Energy Development (CEED), an organisation working in the environmental and energy sectors, has pointed out that extreme heat is causing a significant decline in worker efficiency, resulting in significant losses to the state's Gross State Value Added (GSVA).
The report titled ‘Rising Heat and Economic Impact: Towards a Heat Resilient Jharkhand' was released during a discussion on ‘The Economic Cost of Heat Exposure in Jharkhand’. It states that from 2011-12 to 2022-23, the state has suffered a cumulative economic loss of Rs 1.76 lakh crore (both direct and indirect) due to the impact of heat. This represents approximately 8% of the state's total GSVA. Of this, approximately Rs 0.87 lakh crore was a direct loss.
Workers working in a city in Jharkhand (ETV Bharat) The report has warned that if concrete and appropriate measures are not taken in time, Jharkhand's estimated labour productivity losses could reach Rs 9.35 lakh crore between 2023-24 and 2047-48, accounting for 10.31% of the estimated GSVA, which will include a direct economic loss of Rs 4.70 lakh crore.
The economic losses due to labour productivity caused by heat were most pronounced in sectors that primarily involved outdoor work between 2011-12 to 2022-23. The construction sector accounted for the largest share of losses, at 25&. Agriculture, forestry and fisheries contributed 11%, followed by transport, storage and communications at 10%, manufacturing at 8% and mining at 7%.
Those who carried out the study pointed out that heat doesn't typically cause direct damage to buildings, roads or machinery. Its economic impact is primarily manifested in the form of reduced working hours for outdoor jobs, reduced labour efficiency, construction delays and reduced agricultural production. These losses often go unreported in general economic assessments yet they have a profound impact on the state's economy.
Jharkhand's Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF) and Nodal Officer for Climate Change, Ravi Ranjan, "Visionary planning and timely preventive measures are essential for the safety of workers. Under the State Climate Action Plan, efforts are being made to provide relief and mitigate the effects of heat in vulnerable areas. Immediate and long-term efforts involving communities can further strengthen the climate resilience campaign in the state."
Economist Dr Harishwar Dayal pointed out that a large number of people are engaged in outdoor or physically demanding work. Lack of basic amenities, shade and flexible working hours reduces their efficiency and family income, impacting the overall economy. "This impacts the most vulnerable communities whose livelihoods depend on outdoor work," he said.
Meanwhile, Srishti Pallav, CEED's Director of Policy and Partnerships, stated that this is the first such study to examine the economic losses caused by heat. "Heat resilience planning requires better coordination between various departments and partnerships between industries, businesses and civil society organisations," he underlined.
Shikhar Singh, CEED's Manager of Resilience, who authored the report, stated that this is the first time a report has focused on the impact of heat. He disclosed that the report was based on secondary data.
The document has listed certain recommendations to mitigate the impact of heat on human productivity. It has underlined that no new laws or substantial budgets are required to address this challenge, and damage can be significantly reduced by streamlining existing systems.
It suggests that Jharkhand should develop a comprehensive 'Heat Action Plan' not just focused on health, but also incorporating labour and livelihood security.
All government and private workplaces should be mandated to provide shaded resting areas within a 100 meter radius, free drinking water and a minimum 30-minute break after every 90 minutes of work between 11 AM and 3 PM from April to September.
Under rural development schemes like Viksit Bharat-GRAM G, heavy physical work like soil digging, road construction and tree planting should be carried out during the cooler morning hours from 6 AM to 10 AM and from 4 PM to 6 PM.
Under the Birsa Harit Gram Yojana, shady fruit trees like jackfruit, tamarind and mango should be planted at work sites and along field boundaries so that they provide shade and generate additional income within three to four years. At the same time, local markets and street vendors should be instructed to operate in the morning or late evening to protect them from the scorching heat.

ProCook Q2 sales jump 13.2% despite impact of heatwave
15 October, 2026 | by
Angela Beevers
ProCook has seen its second quarter sales jump by 13.2% to £24.1 million despite the impact of this summer’s heatwave on trading.
In the 16 weeks to 11 October, total like-for-like revenue rose by 6.2%.
Subscribe to TRBRetail revenue increased by 10.6% driven by growth from new store openings. Retail like-for-like revenue edged down 0.7%, however, as the hot weather reduced footfall in the first half of the quarter.
Meanwhile, ecommerce revenue climbed by 17.9%, primarily driven by continued growth in traffic.
The performance meant ProCook delivered record first half revenue of £39.7 million, up 16.3% year-on-year and 8.3% on a like-for-like basis.
The retailer opened three new stores in the first half, along with two relocations and two refits. After two store closures, its retail estate stood at 80 stores at the end of the period, 13 of which are now in its new format.
ProCook said it is well positioned for the upcoming peak trading period and is confident of delivering a full year performance in line with market expectations.
Lee Tappenden, chief executive, said: “Our strategy continues to drive significant market share gains, with trading performance strengthening as we moved through the second quarter following the extreme heat during the summer, to deliver a record first half trading performance.
“Whilst mindful of the unpredictable macro backdrop, we are well positioned for the important peak trading period, with inventory in place across compelling Black Friday and Christmas ranges. We are, therefore, confident in delivering a strong full year performance, in line with market expectations.”

Thiruvananthapuram, 15 Oct (H.S.) :The northeast monsoon is expected to reach Kerala by Thursday evening, with the India Meteorological Department forecasting heavy rainfall across parts of the state until Sunday.
An orange alert has been issued for Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Idukki and Ernakulam districts on Thursday, indicating the possibility of heavy to very heavy rainfall. Residents have been advised to remain vigilant as rain could intensify in isolated areas.
Eight other districts — Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Alappuzha, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode and Wayanad — are under a yellow alert for heavy rainfall on Thursday.
For Friday, yellow alerts have been announced in Pathanamthitta, Idukki, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.
The weather department has also warned of isolated thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and strong winds reaching speeds of up to 40 kilometres per hour. People have been urged to exercise caution during thunderstorms and follow weather updates and safety advisories.
With rainfall expected to strengthen, residents have been advised to avoid all non-essential travel during spells of heavy rain. Particular caution has been urged for those planning journeys through hilly terrain or visits to areas close to rivers and other water bodies.
Authorities have advised people to avoid recreational trips to waterfalls, reservoirs and mountainous areas while adverse weather conditions persist.
The public has also been warned against attempting to cross rivers during heavy rainfall. Entering rivers or other water bodies for bathing or fishing should be strictly avoided when rain intensifies.
The forecast places several districts under rainfall warnings on successive days, making continued vigilance necessary through the weekend. Residents should plan essential journeys around weather conditions and heed instructions issued by local authorities.
As the monsoon arrives, the emphasis remains on limiting exposure to lightning, strong winds and rain-swollen water bodies, particularly during periods of intense rainfall across the affected districts this week.

A mostly clear sky & a warming trend continue. A Heat Advisory is in effect Thursday through Saturday for coastal valleys & beaches, with highs reaching the 80s and 90s. Elevated fire weather concerns
Here's your Central Coast weather forecast from Meteorologist Jim Castillo for San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties.
A mainly clear sky and a warming trend continue. A Heat Advisory is in effect Thursday through Saturday for coastal valleys and beaches, with highs reaching the 80s and 90s. Offshore winds increase Thursday and Friday, bringing elevated fire weather concerns, with a Fire Weather Warning for parts of the Santa Lucia Mountains and into the Los Padres National Forest through interior sections of Santa Barbara County, with gusts up to 40 mph expected.
Many of us will likely see these gusty offshore winds, especially Thursday and Friday morning.
Mountain and forest areas will remain dry with low humidity through the weekend. We begin a cool down on Sunday, but still above-normal temperatures continue into Sunday before a nice cooling trend next week.
Forecast models indicate a much cooler system arriving by midweek, with a slight chance of showers, especially by Wednesday.
